references.text: Moses asks God to blot him out of His book if He does not forgive the people—an early reference to God's book where names are written, corresponding to having one's name written in heaven.
Isaiah speaks of those who are 'written up for life in Jerusalem,' reflecting the idea that the names of the righteous are inscribed with God.
Daniel says that those who are written in the book will be delivered—a parallel to the concept of having one's name written in heaven.
The psalmist speaks of being blotted out of the book of life and not being recorded among the righteous—providing background for the image of names written in heaven.

The immediate context: The disciples rejoice that the spirits obey them, and Jesus gives them authority. In verse 20, Jesus corrects them, saying the real reason to rejoice is that their names are written in heaven.
Paul mentions his fellow workers 'whose names are in the book of life,' which directly corresponds to having one's name written in heaven.
Hebrews speaks of 'the firstborn who are enrolled in heaven,' a direct parallel to Jesus' words about names written in heaven.
Jesus promises the overcomer that his name will not be blotted out from the book of life—corresponding to the image of names written in heaven.
Revelation speaks of the Lamb's book of life, where names are written from the foundation of the world—an elaboration on the idea of heavenly books of names.

The final judgment is based on what is written in the books, and anyone not found in the book of life is thrown into the lake of fire—an eschatological unfolding of having one's name written in heaven.
Only those whose names are written in the Lamb's book of life will enter the new Jerusalem—the ultimate fulfillment of the promise of names written in heaven.
